name: Hydrogen peroxide rinse DIY

lead: The DIY peroxide rinse is a way of whitening teeth and freshening the mouth with diluted pharmacy hydrogen peroxide, usually the 3 percent solution. People use it for a brighter smile and for breath and gum goals.

It borrows from the fact that peroxide, directly or as carbamide peroxide, is the main active ingredient in professional and commercial whitening: it oxidises coloured molecules in the tooth. Whitening products use controlled gels with measured concentrations and contact times, and little published research has tested the home rinse itself. Diluted peroxide rinses have been reviewed for gingivitis and plaque, where they did better than placebo but chlorhexidine was judged much more effective.

paras: People swish a diluted solution around the mouth for a short time and spit it out, usually as an occasional add-on to brushing. Results, where users report them, are gradual and mild since contact time with the teeth is brief. Controlled whitening gels and trays are the usual comparison point.

Sources describe peroxide at 10 percent or more as able to damage tissue and burn mucous membranes, and tooth sensitivity is common with whitening in general. Regulators limit consumer strengths, for example 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide for retail products in the EU, and 3 percent solutions are noted as hazardous to the eyes. Home concentration and contact time are not controlled.

angle.text: Users swish diluted household hydrogen peroxide to lighten teeth and freshen the mouth. Peroxide is the main active ingredient in professional whitening, and the rinse is a low-strength, home version of that idea. Controlled whitening gels have been studied far more than home rinses.

lead: A hydrogen peroxide rinse is a do-it-yourself practice in which diluted household hydrogen peroxide, commonly the 3 percent pharmacy solution, is swished in the mouth, usually for whitening or breath and gum goals. It draws on the fact that hydrogen peroxide, directly or as carbamide peroxide, is the most common active ingredient in tooth whitening [1].

Dilute peroxide rinses have been reviewed for gingivitis and plaque, where they performed better than placebo but chlorhexidine was judged much more effective [2]. For whitening, the evidence concerns controlled gels rather than DIY rinses [1].

Regulators treat consumer peroxide strengths differently: the EU limits retail hydrogen peroxide to 0.1 percent, and up to 6 percent is allowed under professional supervision, while the US FDA endorses gels under 6 percent hydrogen peroxide or up to 16 percent carbamide peroxide [1].

paras: Consumer hydrogen peroxide solutions are usually 3 or 6 percent by weight and sold through pharmacies [2]. Online discussions describe swishing a diluted portion of the 3 percent solution and spitting it out. General dosing or dilution instructions are not given here.

Hydrogen peroxide whitens by free radicals that break down pigment molecules [1]. Studies of whitening cover gels and trays with defined concentrations; the sources reviewed describe no controlled trials of the DIY rinse for whitening.
As a mouth rinse for gum health, reviews cited on Wikipedia found dilute peroxide better than placebo but far less effective than chlorhexidine [2].

Hydrogen peroxide at 10 percent or higher can damage tissue, corrode mucous membranes and cause burning, and poorly fitting trays are among the most common causes of chemical burns in whitening [1]. Whitening commonly causes sensitivity, reported in 67 to 78 percent of people receiving in-office peroxide treatment [1].

Domestic-strength solutions may irritate the eyes and mucous membranes, and a 3 percent solution is described as potentially dangerous to the eye [2]. Carbamide peroxide can increase enamel roughness and porosity, and the long-term effects of concentrations above 6 percent are not clarified [1]. An evaluation cited on the same page found that oral products releasing up to 3.6 percent hydrogen peroxide do not appear to raise cancer risk [1].
No studies found for the home-made rinse specifically. Related research on peroxide whitening gels and peroxide mouthrinses for gingivitis is summarised above [1][2].
